prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms enabled timekeeping at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: the optical lattice clock as the single prize part, credited to Katori and Ye. Round 1 sharpened rather than weakened the case. The decisive physical point is that a magic wavelength makes the lattice Stark shift cancel to first order, so thousands of neutral atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and probed on a narrow optical transition at once. That combines the statistics of an ensemble with the systematic control that previously belonged to a single trapped ion. This is a different mechanism from the frequency comb, which counts optical cycles, and from ion control, which removes motion from one quantum system, and I think that answers the chair's first question: the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly and should not speak of optical clocks or precision spectroscopy in general. The maturity evidence is strong and does not depend on the pending SI decision: independent laboratories operate and compare lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level, and they are used for millimetre-scale redshift measurements and for bounds on varying constants. Six of the eight configurations, including my own, name the same two people, and nobody has proposed a third name or a different pair.
statement.case_against: The objections I take seriously are unchanged and none was removed in round 1. First, a sceptic can still read the lattice clock as a very large step inside a metrology lineage already honoured in 2005 and 2012. I do not agree, for the mechanistic reason above, but the committee should expect that criticism and the citation must meet it. Second, Ludlow, Lemonde, Oates and others who brought lattice clocks to maturity are not credited, and the split between Katori's concept and Ye's performance is intertwined, as Kroll says, so two names are a judgement and not a derivation. Third, my account of the priority sequence is recalled and not checked against a documented source in this exercise, and so is everyone else's, which is why I would keep the citation on the invention and its development and not on a priority claim. Fourth, a prize that is partly justified by metrology is sometimes held back until the SI redefinition is complete; that would be a timing argument and not a scientific one.

responses.point: Proposes B056 together with Hosono's iron-based superconductors (B037) as a two-part prize using exactly three names, arguing the pairing avoids the credit disputes of B007 and B012 and that the open pairing mechanism is an interpretation gap, not a gap in the discovery.
responses.response: I ranked Hosono fourth, so I do not doubt the discovery or its attribution, and I agree the open pairing mechanism is not by itself a bar. My objection is to the pairing, which you concede has almost nothing in common between the parts. A second part chosen because it fits the three-name limit makes the clock prize weaker, not stronger, since the single achievement is already clean and complete with two names. I also note that B037 is a one-person share in a field where Tc-raising work followed quickly in several groups, and no other member has argued for it in round 1. I would keep B056 alone and, to answer the chair's fifth question, if a second part were ever wanted I would look for one that shares a subject with the first, not the one that happens to leave a free seat. On your question about the SI redefinition, I treat it as consequence and coincidence, not as the argument for maturity: the physics was settled by independent comparisons before any decision on the second.

responses.point: Prefers B007 as the sole part, since every member ranked it in their top four, but says that if the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal is judged indispensable then the three-name limit cannot give a fair attribution.
responses.response: That conditional is where I land too, and it is why B007 stays my first alternative and not my preference. You are right that broad ranking across all eight ballots is real information about merit, and I take the point that B007 is the only candidate nobody ranked below fourth. But breadth of ranking does not repair credit: if the BHZ proposal was what made HgTe the platform, the Molenkamp measurement is not independent of it, and any three names leave a visible gap, with Zhang's death making the gap permanent. I cannot settle that from the files, and I think your own wording in round 1 leaves the same question open. I do not see the 2016 prize as a bar, because the Z2 invariant is a distinct step from the quantum Hall lineage, so I am not asking you to give up on the science. I am asking whether you would accept B056 on the grounds that its credit chain is the one that survives the same test.

responses.point: Argues B007 introduced a new organising principle for electronic matter, with Z2 invariants now computed routinely in first-principles work, and treats the BHZ gap as regrettable but not disqualifying because the concept and invariant belong to Kane and Mele.
responses.response: I accept that the Z2 classification changed how band structures are analysed, and your point about routine first-principles use is a stronger consequence argument than I gave it credit for in round 1. Where I differ is on how much the credit gap can be tolerated. A prize is allowed a long tail of uncredited contributors, and I say that of the clock too, but the clock tail consists of groups who followed, whereas the BHZ proposal came before the HgTe measurement and shaped it. That is a different kind of omission. If your citation were limited to the theory of the quantum spin Hall state and the Z2 invariant, naming Kane and Mele, the attribution would be tighter, but then the third name and the HgTe measurement you say supplies the decisive confirmation would fall out, and I would then be comparing a two-person theory prize to a different candidate. I keep B007 as my first alternative and would move it up if the committee could settle the allocation.

responses.point: Wants the citation written around the lattice clock as an invention and its development and not around a priority claim that cannot be verified, and notes that Katori's and Ye's contributions are partly intertwined.
responses.response: I agree and I have changed my citation wording in response: it now names the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 performance and makes no statement about who was first. That also covers your concern about distinguishing it from the comb. One difference remains between us on the verification question. You and I both say we recall the sequence from general knowledge, and in a real committee that would be checked against the primary papers before the vote. I do not think the uncertainty changes the two-name configuration, because whichever way the ordering falls, concept and performance are both in the credited pair, but I would not have the citation depend on it. I also do not agree with raising the Hall connection in your own disclosure as anything more than context; a research stay in a laboratory belonging to the 2005 background is not a tie to Katori or Ye.

responses.point: Ranks the clock above B018 but not by a large margin, because the Jaksch-Zoller proposal, the superfluid-to-Mott experiment and the quantum-gas microscope are separable steps and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems is adjacent.
responses.response: That is a fair correction to my own alternative list, and I accept it. I had B018 second at opening because Bloch, Greiner and Zoller form a strong, coherent trio, but I did not weigh enough that the decisive step is arguable and that microscope work was extended by others. I keep it as my second alternative only because it is the nearest candidate in subject and maturity to the clock, not because I think it is ready to compete this year. Your many-body remark on the clock is also useful. Collisional shifts and collective effects were part of reaching the 10^-18 level, which is part of why credit for the performance step belongs with the group that controlled them. I would not add a third name for that reason, since that work was done inside the same group.

responses.point: Moved to B056 as the preferred configuration, accepting that the comb prize honoured an enabling technology, and argues that broadening credit to the clock community would require a third name which the evidence does not obviously support.
responses.response: I agree with keeping it at two names, and I appreciate that you moved from IceCube after weighing the arguments and said so. On B003, which you keep as an alternative, my position is as in round 1: two names cannot honestly represent a collaboration of that scale or the AMANDA and DUMAND predecessors, and the source identification of the astrophysical flux is still at moderate significance. I have not seen in round 1 a statement of which contributions by Halzen and Karle were decisive for the discovery as distinct from construction, which was what I asked for. So I leave B003 out of my alternatives. As chair you also took part in the leading position, which you have disclosed; I do not think that is a problem for the discussion, but it is useful to have it on the record.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes; I believe the magic-wavelength mechanism makes it distinct, but this is a judgement.
The priority sequence between Katori's concept and the first lattice-clock demonstrations is recalled and not checked against primary papers, and I would want it checked before the citation is final.
Whether two names are enough given the contributions of Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates and others, and whether the performance credit to Ye and the concept credit to Katori can be cleanly separated.
Whether the committee holds back a metrology prize until the SI redefinition of the second is concluded, which I regard as timing and not science.
Whether the BHZ proposal was indispensable to the HgTe measurement; if it was not, B007 would move to the front of my list, and this is the main way my position could still change.
statement.conflict_note: No direct connection to Katori or Ye is documented in my profile, nor to the other credited names on the shortlist. My documented connections (training in Lindgren's Gothenburg group, collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH, and work with Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato) concern attosecond photoionisation and storage-ring physics and not lattice clocks. I work in the same broad atomic-physics community as B056 and B018, and I disclose that field proximity again; I see no specific conflict that requires recusal or abstention, and I do not advise one for any other member on the information in the round-1 files.
